nodes.title: Convert volume units
nodes.refresher:
## Convert before substituting
A litre is 1000 millilitres, and 1 mL equals 1 cm³. To convert length in a volume formula, cube the length conversion too. One metre is 100 centimetres, so one cubic metre contains one million cubic centimetres.

:::exercise Track the cubic unit
Convert 0.36 L to cubic centimetres.
:::answer
Multiply 0.36 by 1000 to get 360 cm³.
:::end

nodes.title: Calculate mass density
nodes.refresher:
## Keep mass and volume separate
Density is mass divided by volume. Choose the requested mass and volume units before substituting. If the mass is in grams and density is needed in grams per cubic centimetre, convert the volume to cubic centimetres first.

:::exercise Convert and divide
A sample has mass 84 g and volume 0.024 L. Find its density in g cm⁻³.
:::answer
Convert the volume to 24 cm³. The density is 84 divided by 24, or 3.5 g cm⁻³.
:::end

nodes.title: Preserving equality
nodes.refresher:
## Keep the balance
Imagine two equal loads. Changing one load alone destroys the balance. A reversible operation on both sides preserves the solution set; multiplying both sides by zero loses information.

:::exercise Try a fresh equation
Solve $5z+4=24$ without changing the balance.
:::answer
Subtract 4 on both sides to obtain $5z=20$, then divide both sides by the nonzero number 5: $z=4$. Check: $5(4)+4=24$.
:::end

Pause and predict: why would multiplying both sides by zero prevent recovering the original equation?

nodes.title: Combining powers of one base
nodes.refresher:
## Count the factors
For positive real $x$, multiplying powers of the same base combines their factors: $x^m x^n=x^{m+n}$. This is a product rule for powers, not a rule for adding powers.

:::exercise Combine first
Simplify $x^4x^5$ for positive $x$.
:::answer
There are nine factors of $x$, so the product is $x^9$. In contrast, $x^4+x^5$ is a sum and cannot be combined by adding exponents.
:::end

Before differentiating, distinguish a product from a sum. Assumptions matter when extending exponent laws beyond positive bases.

nodes.title: Limit versus function value
nodes.refresher:
## Nearby behaviour
A missing reading at one input does not erase the trend of nearby readings. A limit concerns admissible inputs approaching the target from both sides; it does not assign a value at a missing point.

:::exercise A hole in the rule
Find the limit as $t$ approaches 9 of $(t^2-81)/(t-9)$, where $t\ne9$.
:::answer
Factor and cancel only on the punctured domain: $(t-9)(t+9)/(t-9)=t+9$. The nearby values approach 18. The original expression is still undefined at 9.
:::end

Predict: would assigning a new value at just $t=9$ change this limit?

nodes.title: Differentiating a power
nodes.refresher:
## A local rate
The derivative measures local output change per unit input change. For a positive integer $n$, the power rule compresses the difference-quotient argument: the derivative of $x^n$ is $nx^{n-1}$.

:::exercise Keep both changes
Differentiate $7x^4$.
:::answer
Keep the constant multiplier, multiply by the original exponent, then reduce the exponent by one: $28x^3$. Both the coefficient and exponent change.
:::end

For position as a function of time, its derivative is velocity. This is a general physical analogy, not a retrieved physics lesson.

connections.label: Rate of change and velocity
connections.text: A position-time derivative is velocity; units change from distance to distance per time. This general analogy does not imply enrollment in physics.

nodes.title: Differentiating a composition
nodes.refresher:
## Two linked changes
If $y=f(g(x))$, a small change passes through the inner and outer functions. Under differentiability assumptions the chain rule multiplies the two local rates: $f'(g(x))g'(x)$.

:::exercise Follow the inner change
Differentiate $(4x+1)^3$.
:::answer
The outer derivative gives $3(4x+1)^2$. The inner derivative is 4, so the full result is $12(4x+1)^2$.
:::end

Check whether an expression is a composition before selecting the rule.

nodes.title: Recovering a rate from accumulation
nodes.refresher:
## Accumulation remembers a rate
Let $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$. If $f$ is continuous near the input under consideration, a small change in the upper endpoint adds a thin signed slice, and $F'(x)=f(x)$.

:::exercise Read the endpoint
For $F(x)=\int_2^x(3t+4)\,dt$, find $F'(5)$.
:::answer
The variable is the upper endpoint, so the fundamental theorem gives $F'(x)=3x+4$ and $F'(5)=19$.
:::end

An endpoint $g(x)$ would also require a chain-rule factor; reversing the limits changes the sign.

nodes.title: Reversible row replacement
nodes.refresher:
## Preserve the same solutions
A row represents a whole equation. Replacing a row by itself plus a multiple of another row is reversible, so it preserves the solution set. Apply the operation to the augmented entry too.

:::exercise Include the last column
With $R_1=[1,2\mid5]$ and $R_2=[3,7\mid18]$, compute $R_2-3R_1$.
:::answer
Operate entry by entry, including the right-hand side: $[0,1\mid3]$. Leaving the last column unchanged would describe a different system.
:::end

A contradiction row and a free-variable row tell different solution stories.

nodes.title: The two-by-two determinant
nodes.refresher:
## Signed area scaling
For a two-by-two matrix with rows $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$, the determinant is $ad-bc$. Its magnitude scales area; its sign records orientation. A zero determinant means the transformation collapses area and has no inverse.

:::exercise Keep the subtraction order
Find the determinant of $\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\2&5\end{bmatrix}$.
:::answer
The determinant is $3(5)-1(2)=13$. An inverse exists because this determinant is nonzero.
:::end

A row swap changes the determinant sign. An elementary row replacement preserves it.
